slides.title: Introduction to Model Context Protocols
bullets: Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI models access external systems and context.
Eliminates custom one-off integration glue code for every developer tool and repository.
Enables seamless discovery of local tools, file systems, and external service APIs.
slides.notes: Welcome to week 2. In our previous week, we explored general developer workflows with AI assistance. Today, we delve into Model Context Protocols, an open architecture that allows language models to interface safely and consistently with workspace tools, databases, and services. MCP standardizes context ingestion so developers do not need bespoke integration code for every single tool.

slides.title: Why Standardization of Context Matters
bullets: Non-standardized context leads to fragmented tool APIs and fragile prompt engineering.
Standardized schemas ensure consistent tool signatures and reliable response handling.
Uniform protocols decouple the AI client from underlying language runtimes and environments.

figure.caption: Custom Integration vs Standardized MCP Architecture
rows: Standard JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP

slides.notes: Before standardized protocols, connecting an LLM to local file systems or developer tools required custom extensions for each editor or framework. MCP provides a universal interface. Like Language Server Protocol revolutionized code editors, MCP standardizes how AI models read resources, invoke tools, and retrieve context prompts across diverse developer environments.

slides.title: High-Level Architecture of Model Context Protocol
bullets: Follows a clean client-server architecture inside the developer workspace.
Hosts encapsulate the AI application such as an IDE or CLI tool.
Clients maintain isolated connections with MCP servers handling specific domains.
slides.notes: The architecture separates concerns into Host, Client, Server, and Resources. The Host is the top-level application, such as VS Code or an AI CLI. The Client lives inside the Host and manages communication. The MCP Server exposes specific capabilities—like reading git history or running unit tests—via standardized protocol messages.

slides.title: MCP Host, Client, and Server Roles
bullets: MCP Host controls application UI, user permissions, and AI orchestration.
MCP Client initiates protocol handshakes and routes requests to designated servers.
MCP Server implements capabilities like resources, prompts, and executable tools.
slides.notes: Understanding these roles is crucial for workspace configuration. The MCP Host acts as the container. It spawns MCP Clients, which establish connections to individual MCP Servers. Each server operates independently in its own process, exposing resources or executable functions while adhering to strict context protocol rules.

slides.title: Communication Transports: Stdio vs WebSockets and HTTP
bullets: Stdio transport launches local server subprocesses via standard input and output channels.
HTTP with Server-Sent Events connects remote or containerized MCP servers.
Both transports serialize protocol messages using standard JSON-RPC 2.0 format.
slides.notes: MCP supports two primary transport mechanisms. Local workspace setups typically use stdio, where the client spawns the server binary directly as a subprocess and communicates over standard input and output. For remote or cloud-hosted tools, HTTP with Server-Sent Events or WebSockets is used. Regardless of transport, the payload structure remains identical JSON-RPC 2.0.

slides.title: Core MCP Schema: Server Capabilities
bullets: Servers declare supported features during initial handshake capability negotiation.
Main capability primitives include resources, prompts, and tools.
Capability declarations prevent clients from sending unsupported requests to servers.
slides.notes: During the initialize exchange, the server sends its capability manifest. This JSON payload lists what the server can handle: whether it provides static context resources, pre-configured prompts, or dynamic executable tools. If a capability is absent, the client knows not to query that feature.

slides.title: MCP Schema: Defining Resources
bullets: Resources expose contextual data like files, database schemas, or logs to the AI.
Expressed using URI templates such as file system paths or custom schemes.
Resources can be static files or dynamic streams updated via subscription events.
slides.notes: Resources are passive data items that the LLM can attach to its context window. Each resource is identified by a unique URI. When an AI agent needs context about a project, it requests resource contents via the server's resource endpoints.

slides.title: MCP Schema: Defining Tools and Arguments
bullets: Tools represent executable functions that perform side effects or computations.
Schema requires exact tool names, descriptions, and JSON Schema input parameters.
Client validates LLM arguments against JSON Schema before invoking the server tool.
slides.notes: Tools allow the AI model to interact dynamically with the developer workspace—for example, running test suites or formatting code. Tool definitions must strictly follow JSON Schema standards for input parameters so the client can validate the model's output before executing standard functions.

slides.title: MCP Schema: Defining Prompts and Context Templates
bullets: Prompts are predefined template messages designed for recurring developer workflows.
Accept typed parameters to dynamically populate workspace context into prompts.
Helps standardize prompt engineering patterns across an entire development team.

figure.caption: MCP Prompt Definition Schema

slides.notes: Prompts in MCP are reusable workflow templates. Instead of copy-pasting complex system prompts, developers configure prompt templates on the MCP server. The host UI can then surface these prompts with parameterized dropdowns or text inputs.

slides.title: Concept Check: MCP Roles and Capabilities

quiz.question: Which component in the Model Context Protocol architecture is responsible for initiating handshakes and executing JSON Schema validation on AI tool calls?
quiz.explanation: The MCP Client acts as the bridge inside the Host app; it manages protocol connections, handshakes, and validates tool arguments against JSON Schema before sending requests. The Host handles UI/UX, while the Server exposes capabilities.

slides.notes: Pause for 5 minutes. Have students answer this question to check their understanding of host versus client versus server duties in MCP architecture.

slides.title: Inspecting an MCP Workspace Configuration File
bullets: Workspace configurations register available MCP servers and their launch parameters.
Uses standard JSON format defining server keys, executable commands, and arguments.
Environment variables pass necessary paths and authentication tokens safely.
slides.notes: Here is an example workspace configuration file. Notice the top-level key mcpServers. Each entry defines a server key, the binary command to execute, and command-line args. This standard structure allows the client to spawn stdio subprocesses automatically.

slides.title: Protocol Requirements: JSON-RPC 2.0 Message Structure
bullets: All communications adhere strictly to the JSON-RPC 2.0 specification.
Request messages include jsonrpc, id, method, and optional params.
Response messages return matching id, and either result or an error object.
slides.notes: Under the hood, MCP messages travel as line-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 payloads. Each request carries a unique ID, which the server echoes back in its response. This asynchronous request-response pairing guarantees order tracking across stdio and HTTP streams.

slides.title: Parsing Requests and Responses in JSON-RPC
bullets: Demonstrates handling JSON-RPC requests for resource retrieval.
Server verifies URI path validity and returns structured resource content.
Explicit path resolution avoids broken or missing template path strings.
slides.notes: Notice how this slide explicitly specifies literal URI paths like file:///workspace/config.json without any unfilled template variables. The request asks to read a specific resource, and the server returns a result array with text content and MIME type.

slides.title: Managing Security, Permissions, and Access Control
bullets: MCP tools execute arbitrary code; hosts must enforce strict access boundaries.
Workspace configurations must restrict server access to explicitly defined roots.
User confirmation prompts are required before non-read-only tool execution.
slides.notes: Security is a core architectural requirement. Because MCP servers can run subprocesses or modify local files, the client and host must enforce security boundaries. Workspace configs should limit directory paths accessible to server binaries, and the host UI must require user consent before executing side-effecting tools.

slides.title: Common Configuration Warnings and Protocol Mismatches
bullets: Protocol version mismatch during initialization handshake causes connection rejection.
Schema validation errors trigger warnings if tool argument types do not match.
Misconfigured command paths lead to immediate stdio process exit errors.

figure.caption: Debugging Common Workspace Configuration Errors
rows: Client and Server MCP versions differ
Update server package or client version
Fix schema types in tool definition
Command binary or path not found
Verify executable command and environment args

slides.notes: When setting up a workspace template, you will frequently encounter configuration warnings. Common issues include unsupported protocol versions during the handshake, invalid JSON Schema in tool definitions, or incorrect executable paths in the configuration JSON.

slides.title: Validating Workspace Templates Against MCP Schema
bullets: Auditing a configuration for schema compliance and protocol readiness.
Validates structural correctness of mcpServers JSON block.
Ensures required environment variables and path arguments are supplied.
slides.notes: In this example, we see a complete, schema-compliant server configuration. The key database_inspector defines standard command, args, and env properties. Validating your JSON configuration against the official schema prevents startup errors and ensures smooth tool discovery.

slides.title: Concept Check: Configuration and Protocol Diagnostics

quiz.question: A developer receives a runtime warning stating 'Tool invocation failed: input parameter does not match schema'. Which component is failing validation?
options: The client validation of LLM arguments against the server tool JSON Schema
The server URI string format in the prompt resource request
The initial handshake protocol version string
quiz.explanation: When an LLM generates tool arguments, the MCP Client validates those arguments against the server's published JSON Schema before sending the JSON-RPC call. Failure indicates the LLM output violates parameter types specified in the tool schema.

slides.notes: Pause for 5 minutes. Conduct this check to verify that students can diagnose schema validation errors during tool calls.

slides.title: Summary: Model Context Protocols and Architecture
bullets: MCP standardizes context sharing and tool invocation between AI hosts and servers.
Architecture relies on Hosts, Clients, and Servers communicating via JSON-RPC 2.0.
Schema definitions cover Resources, Tools, and Prompts with strict JSON Schema rules.
Proper workspace configuration prevents runtime protocol mismatches and security risks.
slides.notes: To summarize today's lecture, Model Context Protocols provide a robust standard for connecting AI tools to developer workspaces. By understanding host-client-server roles, JSON-RPC 2.0 messages, and schema validation rules, you can configure developer workspace templates error-free and ready for automated coding workflows.
